spent the weekend on a problem probably nobody cares about:

👉 agents can't draw geometrically correct vector paths

ask one to draw a line through a logo and it will fail

also, ever seen apple's "hello" handwriting animation? 

to make one, something has to trace a single clean line through the shape

but agents just guess the path, and the guess is almost always wrong 

I thought, if I give it the correct tools and workflows, it can do it every single time

so I spent the weekend on single line vectorization for text-to-lottie to get clean mask-reveal animations from SVG logos

here's the problem. logos are almost never single line paths/strokes. they are filled shapes with multiple contours, folded forms, sharp or rounded corners, rails, caps and tight apexes

we use trim paths to reveal a stroke along a single path. but a filled logo doesn’t have one

so before you can animate the reveal, you have to derive a precise mask path down the center of the shape first. that's the actual hard part

agents commonly just guess that path and draw very bad ones, and mostly fail, since there is no guided good workflow for it

this is a common issue when you ask to redraw something

so I explored a bunch of different methods to extract a clean path line, by thinking about how a human actually does it

explored a bunch of different workflows in figma and tested those approaches in text-to-lottie

after choosing one of those workflows, I needed a repeatable geometric method

the method, at a high level:

- start from the SVG source (if it's a PNG, vectorize it to SVG first)
- read the actual SVG path data and structure first (no screenshot)
- analyze its boundaries, rails, contours, turns, caps and intersections
- then derive a measured centerline from the geometry

it relies on contour rail pairing, not skeletonization

skeletonization is the usual approach, but it is not always clean

it pulls away from sharp corners and often creates extra branches (extra path splits), so we only use it as a fallback when the shape is actually branched

for these tests, I needed to pick a logo that covers all those hard cases

that's why I picked this flag mark from wise

the key insight: 

a folded logo is one closed outline that loops, out along one rail and back along the other

the extraction step works like this:

1. find the caps, the U turns where the outline reverses

the number of caps tells us what kind of shape we're dealing with

- two caps = one strip with two ends
- folded ribbon = that strip bends back on itself

2. split the shape at the caps into two rails

then pair the rails by route order, not arc length, because folds break arc length

3. check how sharp or curved the shape is

- if it has sharp corners, meet the centerlines at the corner
- if it is curved, project across the rails so the line stays stable through folds

4. refine the centerline, clean up the path, make the mask fit the logo's fill width and choose the starting cap so the reveal animation begins from the right end

then verification : the agent builds a geometry sandbox

at first, the geometry sandbox rule lived in the skill’s md file. then I moved it into scripts

because a written rule can tell the agent what to do, but it can still interpret that rule in different ways (which it did lol)

it can't prove the path is actually centered every time

so the rule is:

for any nontrivial filled mark, the agent has to build a runnable sandbox that produces real file artifacts before touching the Lottie scene

so the flow is:

1. start with the SVG
2. run derive_rails.py to extract the rails and centerline
3. output centerline.json + centerline.svg : verify the geometry
4. use the verified centerline to build the Lottie scene

btw, the centerline.svg is required for the human check 

it opens in any SVG preview with no dev server, so the person using it sees the exact derived shape, gives revisions if needed 

both agent and human confirm it visually from the SVG source (which I'll share some of them in the thread)

so far the results are very good. for the logo animations I've created, the agent simply couldn't produce these before

for comparison:
- previous version: unable to create mask paths. too many detailed instructions and longer conversations, a 5+ hr claude code session with back and forth, still wasn't enough

you had to draw the path yourself on figma and give it to the agent to animate it

- current version: one shot prompt, short and no details, done in ~10 minutes + no revision required

currently finalizing the mask reveal workflow for logos, and planning the next part: handwritten text animations

Someone ran one prompt for 12 hours and got what he calls personal AGI. 

Every call, email, and doc about his life and business, now queryable in one place. 

And it is one of 8 things that dropped last week most people slept on. Me and @AndrewWarner broke them all down in the video below. 

Here's what you need to know:

1. Record and Replay shipped in Codex. Do a task once and it builds a skill it runs for you from then on. Biggest update last week, no contest.

2. @nickvasiles ran a /goal prompt in Codex for 12 hours and built a second brain of his whole business. Every transcript and connector, queryable. He gave the prompt away free.

3. Anthropic put Claude in Slack with Tag. Your team @-mentions it and it pulls Salesforce, chases error spikes, and posts a Monday pipeline digest. Team and Enterprise plans only.

4. WorkClaw makes OpenClaw a one-click install for Slack and Teams. Spin up specialized agents and let them talk with a checkbox. Two weeks of setup, now two clicks.

5. BlueRails makes your site readable to AI agents, then lets them check out on it. The pay-with-PayPal button, but for agents. Six to twelve months early, so now is the time to get ready.

6. OpenRouter shipped an MCP that picks your model for you. Ask for the best coding model under $2 per million tokens and it routes you live. GLM 5.2 keeps winning on cost.

7. Dump raw meeting transcripts into Codex and one-shot the tool you talked about. One note became a working ROI calculator.

8. Zapier MCP gives your agent its own logins with permissions you set. Let it draft email but never send. Google's version took an hour and failed. This took minutes.

2 things I find interesting here:

1. Your context is the moat, not the model. Models are a commodity now. The queryable knowledge base of your business is the one asset that survives every model swap. Start building your second brain this week.

2. The winning agents live where your team already works. Slack, Teams, your inbox, your site. Stop waiting for people to open a new app and put the agent where the work happens.

We covered all of it (plus the tool that called Andrew a pro poker player and a one-shot menu bar app for watching the World Cup while you work) on this week's News You Missed.

THIS GUY FOUND A FREE LOCAL DASHBOARD FOR CLAUDE CODE TOKEN BURN

Most Claude Code users only notice tokens when the limit warning shows up.

CodeBurn is useful because it shows the burn pattern before that moment.

It is a free, open-source, local dashboard for AI coding usage.

The video shows it breaking spend down by:

> project
> model
> activity type
> sessions
> shell commands

That matters because “Claude feels expensive today” is not an engineering signal.

“This project is burning tokens on exploration” is.

“This session kept retrying the same failure” is.

“This model was overkill for the task” is.

The best metric in the demo is the one-shot rate.

Simple idea:

Did Claude solve the task on the first attempt, or did it spiral into retries, debugging, rewriting, and tool calls?

A low one-shot rate is not just a cost problem.

It usually points to a workflow problem:

bad spec
unclear context
missing tests
too much repo noise
wrong model for the job
blind retries instead of narrowing the task

That is the real reason this kind of dashboard matters.

It does not magically make Claude cheaper.

It gives you the receipt.

You still have to change the behavior: smaller tasks, cleaner context, better prompts, better specs, cheaper models when possible, and fewer “try again” loops.

But if Claude Code is part of your daily dev loop, that receipt is valuable.

The next layer for AI coding is not only smarter agents.

It is observability for agents.

Once the assistant becomes part of the engineering workflow, token spend stops being just a billing line.

It becomes a debugging signal.

Claude Code loops are simpler than everyone makes them sound.

I broke down every piece across real builds and live testing.

Here's the full system:

1/ What a Loop Is
> A recurring task that keeps running until the job is done
> Not a one-shot prompt. Not a pipeline. A persistent agent with a goal.
> It checks completion after every pass and decides whether to stop or go again

2/ How It Differs From a Routine
> A routine is linear. Step 1, step 2, step 3, done. Think Zapier.
> A loop is circular. It finishes a pass, checks its goal, and starts again if needed
> Routines stop. Loops stop only when the end state is met.

3/ What Makes Up a Loop
> Goal: the north star the entire loop works toward
> Prompts: the instructions for each pass
> Tools: whatever Claude needs to actually do the work
> Memory: context carried between passes
> End state: the specific condition that kills the loop

4/ Loop Rules
> Minimum frequency: every 1 minute
> Hard limit: 3 days max before everything stops
> Cost reality: every pass burns tokens. 10-minute loops over 3 days adds up fast.
> Keep prompts tight. Vague loops = expensive loops.

5/ Use Case 1: PR Review Loop
> /loop every 10 minutes
> Review every new pull request. Check diff for bugs and regressions. Fix what you find. Commit back to the same PR.
> End state: tests pass, lint is clean, CI is green.

6/ Use Case 2: Internal Tool From Spec
> /loop every 10 minutes
> Read the spec doc. Build the next missing piece. Write tests for it.
> End state: every item in the spec is built and all tests pass.
> You set it, walk away, and come back to a working app.

The whole point of loops: stop babysitting your AI.

Define the goal. Define done. Let it run.

The best engineers aren't prompting harder. They're looping smarter.
